title: Andersen et al., The Impact of Tutorials on Games of Varying Complexity (CHI 2012)
label: research
claim: Eight tutorial designs in three games, 45,000+ players. Tutorials raised play time up to 29% (progress up to 75%) in the most complex game (Foldit); no significant engagement gain in the two simpler games. Authors: tutorial investment may not be justified where mechanics can be discovered by experiment. Project page does not list the eight designs.

title: Different types of Tutorials (Game Developer)
label: practitioner
claim: Distinguishes instructions, examples, and a carefully designed experience (SMB 1-1). Tutorial value depends on game complexity; active-learning tutorials fail when the player has no isolated place to practise a complex skill; Braid shows its rewind help after the first death, i.e. when first necessary; no single best method. Does not address skipping. 2026-11-08 verification read: active-learning tutorials 'may be ineffective when the player never has an isolated place to practice a particularly complex skill' (hedged, not 'fail'); Braid's tutorial 'only appears based on a certain event, i.e. the player's death'; the page cites Hearts of Iron 3 as teaching 'the player everything before they could play'.

title: Design Philosophy: Shigeru Miyamoto (blakecrosley.com)

title: Expertise reversal effect / worked-example search results
label: research
claim: Guidance that helps novices becomes redundant and harmful for those with more knowledge (Kalyuga); unguided search loads novices' working memory; remedy in the literature is fading supports adaptively. One legal-reasoning study found no reversal for less-structured tasks. No game-specific study seen.

title: Portal developer commentary transcript (fan wiki hosting Valve's in-game commentary)

Davis: testers assumed orange portals were exit-only, so a puzzle was added. Chin: playtesting showed a puzzle 'introduced too many new concepts at once'. Barnett: 'without some serious prompting, players will rarely look up.' Transcript hosted by a wiki, speech is Valve's.

title: Thinking with Portals: Making a Test Chamber (Game Informer, 2010)
label: developer
claim: Valve trains in two stages: 'checklisting' breaks a new mechanic into the core components players must grasp, in 'a very clean room to safely experiment with it'; then challenges 'take a previously learned rule and turn it on its head'. Playtesting is how they verify the teaching worked; when testers miss a required element the element is made more noticeable.

title: Andersen et al., Impact of Tutorials on Games of Varying Complexity (CHI 2012), full PDF
label: research
claim: 45,000+ players, 8 conditions, Refraction, Hello Worlds, Foldit. Foldit: tutorials raised play time up to 29%, progress up to 75%; negligible effect in the other two. Context-sensitive instructions: +16% play time, +40% progress in Foldit, no effect elsewhere. No evidence that restricting freedom helps. On-demand help helped Foldit, no effect in Hello Worlds, NEGATIVE in Refraction. Conclusion: players of experimentable games seem to learn more from experimentation than from reading text.

title: Iwata Asks: New Super Mario Bros. Wii, Vol 1 part 4 (Nakago, Tezuka, Iwata), full page
label: developer
claim: Nakago: levels were not made from screen one; World 3 or 5 came first, and beginners found them incredibly difficult, so 'our basic principle is to move easier features to the beginning of the level'. 1-1 was designed so the player always gets the mushroom (first pipe placed because the mushroom bounces off it); planned on paper with fallback paths; created at the end and adjusted until the last minute. Iwata: at release players did not read the manual, so the game was built for beginners to learn naturally. The page does not say Miyamoto described the forced mushroom as showing it differs from a Goomba.

title: Kalyuga 2007, Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction (Educ Psychol Rev), full PDF
label: research
claim: Designs effective for low-knowledge learners can lose effect or have negative consequences for proficient ones. Conclusion: replicated across many materials and participants (2,200+ students; effect sizes 0.45 to 2.99), full reversal or more often partial; reversal usually shown cross-sectionally; guidance should be given at the appropriate time and unnecessary support removed as learners progress; adaptive tailoring has best potential. Limits: few studies of optimal methods, mostly well-defined technical domains.

title: Microsoft, Xbox Accessibility Guideline 116: Time limits (XAG, current)
read: full (via fetch summarizer; quotes as returned)
label: guideline
claim: For tutorial windows, speaker dialogue and similar timed elements: "Allow the player to adjust the number of seconds these elements appear (in settings), up to at least 10x the default." Or "allow the player to disable duration limits entirely so elements can be dismissed or advanced on input." Examples: Ori and the Will of the Wisps keeps NPC dialogue on screen until A is pressed; Dragon Quest XI S Autoplay Cutscenes toggle. Does NOT say the timer is forbidden; it is an adjust-or-disable requirement, and it does not mention re-showing a missed lesson.

title: W3C, Understanding SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (WCAG 2.2)
label: guideline
claim: SC 2.2.1: for each content-set time limit the user can turn it off, adjust it to at least ten times the default, or "be warned before time expires and given at least 20 seconds to extend". Understanding doc: "animated, moving or scrolling content introduces a time limit on a user's ability to read content". Toast example: a message that disappears after 5 seconds sets no time limit if users can learn the same information another way; "if the user has no other means of discovering the same information" the SC applies. That last point is the closest support for 'a timed lesson needs another route back'. Written for web content, not games; exceptions for real-time events and essential limits. I did not read 2.2.2/2.2.3.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Allow players to progress through text prompts at their own pace (Cognitive, Basic)
label: guideline
claim: "It is not possible to set a speed for text to be displayed which will be appropriate for all readers"; distraction can cause players to miss key information. Recommends "Instead of a timer, dismiss information on a player action, allowing it to be stepped through"; if infeasible, let players replay or pause the text; in chat let players scroll back. Examples: Doom weapon info, Guacamelee! in-game text, Happy Wars instructions. Basic level. Does not mention phone glancing specifically. I did not find the exact 'no essential information only in timed text' wording; this is the nearest entry.

title: Oulasvirta, Tamminen, Roto, Kuorelahti, Interaction in 4-second bursts: the fragmented nature of attentional resources in mobile HCI (CHI 2005)
read: full text (pdftotext of the PDF; abstract and discussion read)
label: research
claim: Field study, web-search tasks on a phone across nine urban situations. Abstract: "spans of over 16 seconds in a laboratory condition dropping to bursts of just a few seconds in difficult mobile situations". Discussion: continuous attention "fragmented and broke down to bursts of just 4 to 8 seconds, and attention to the mobile device had to be interrupted by glancing the environment up to 8 times during a subtask of waiting a Web page to be loaded." Walking/moving participants, web search task, small sample; says nothing about game prompts. Title says 4-second, body says 4 to 8 seconds.

title: Game Developer, Behavior analysis of 50,000 mobile players (Thermometers Puzzles)

title: Kao, Magana, Mousas, Evaluating Tutorial-Based Instructions for Controllers in VR Games (PACM HCI / CHI PLAY, 2021)
read: full text (pdftotext), abstract and Table 2, methods skimmed
label: research
claim: Four between-subjects experiments, four VR games, 433 participants (108/111/100/114, ~31-40 per cell, Mechanical Turk, 370 male/63 female, headset owners). Three tutorial modalities: Text, Text+Diagram, Text+Spatial (tooltips on the virtual controllers). Third-person shooter: Text+Spatial significantly higher controls learnability than Text and Text+Diagram, and higher performance, player experience and intrinsic motivation than Text. Puzzle game: Text+Spatial > Text on learnability and performance; Text+Diagram > Text on learnability. Wave shooter and rhythm game: 'differences between conditions were negligible'. Conclusion: modality matters by game type. Related work in it: Frommel et al. compared all-instructions-before-practice with just-in-time in a VR wave shooter and found just-in-time gave higher positive emotions, lower negative emotions and higher motivation. Does NOT test no-tutorial vs tutorial; controllers-learning only; crowd sample, no retention measure. Frommel result is as reported by Kao, original paper not read.

title: Passalacqua, Morin, Senecal, Nacke, Leger, Demystifying the first-time experience of mobile games (Multimodal Technologies and Interaction 4(3), 2020)
read: full text extracted, front matter and methods start only; findings from abstract
label: research
claim: Title/abstract: presence of a tutorial has a positive impact on non-expert players' flow and continuous-use intentions. Design: participants randomly assigned to tutorial vs no tutorial; 40 most extreme players picked from ~250 screened (20 lowest and 20 highest weekly playtime), electrodermal activity plus self-report. So n=40 total, ~10 per cell, one mobile game, flow and intent-to-continue measured, not actual retention. Partly disputes onboarding.md's 'no measurable effect in simpler games': here a tutorial helped novices (Andersen found no effect on engagement in simple games); the two differ in outcome measure and sample. Experts showed no benefit by the title's framing (not verified in text).

title: Josh Strife Hayes, How to Design a Tutorial (Josh Strife Plays, YouTube, 2022-07-05)
label: practitioner
claim: Four tests: (1) explain a mechanic and let the player use it immediately in safety ('information given flows directly into the next player action'); information the player cannot use yet is forgotten (Deus Ex: Human Revolution's 90-second inventory video); (2) stack mechanics least to most complex, and the first time actions combine say so ('a brand new player won't know the previous learned actions have synergy'); standalone mechanics are 'a gallery of what the designer has chosen to put in'; (3) deliver tutorial information in the game's own narrative channel (Dark Souls' orange messages, Dead Space's suit hologram); (4) make it the opening, not a separate area; naming a level 'tutorial' signals it doesn't matter. Walkthroughs of Dark Souls, DXHR, Dead Space, Portal (big arrows at the portal gun; two-cube room teaches looking up or down; no 'look up' sign mentioned), Morrowind, Soul Reaver. Dark Souls gaps: kindling and reverse hollowing never taught; 'many people have completed the game without knowing what these things do'. Item shine teaches because the first shine was on the key. Critic's analysis, no player data.

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [03:00]
label: developer

label: developer

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [10:00]
label: developer

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [11:00]

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [12:00]
label: developer

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [14:00]

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [15:00]

label: developer
claim: Rejected fixes for the sunflower problem: tower-defense auto income (sunflowers 'too iconic'), tutorial text like 'Sun is like fuel' (done 'a little bit'), starting with a column of sunflowers (novices might not adapt when it stops), reserved sunflower tiles (adds complexity). Preferred a solution within the rules (19:00-21:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [22:00]
label: developer
claim: Fix via cost and highlight: sunflower cost changed to 50 and starting sun to 50 so only the sunflower is lit at level start; 'the first thing you're gonna do is likely to plant a sunflower'. Cheaper sunflower also lights more often. He credits Fisher-Price: 'press the bright shiny object' (22:00-23:00). Makes it a game rule so hardcore players don't feel they are on easy mode (24:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [25:00]
label: developer
claim: Initial recharge applied to walnut/potato mine and other slow plants so nothing else is lit at level start; for the first ten levels the sunflower is the only highlighted plant at the start. Changing the cost forced rebalancing and replaying the whole game about three times (24:00-26:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [26:00]
label: developer
claim: Eight-word rule, his wording: 'a maximum of eight words on the screen at any given moment'. It is a personal rule of thumb, not measured: 'pretty much impossible to maintain and I do break the rule from time to time but... a good thing to shoot for' (26:00). Also keep messages to few sentences (27:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [27:00]
label: developer
claim: Evidence on reading is his intuition, not data: with a four-sentence message 'I think it's more likely they're going to read zero... when we see a big block of text we tend to tune out'; he says he himself fast-forwards past such blocks (27:00). Shipped one-sentence message: 'click on a seed packet to pick it up'.

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [28:00]
label: developer
claim: Plant descriptions are one sentence containing the most decision-relevant fact: sunflower 'gives you an additional Sun', cherry bomb 'blows up all zombies in an area', fume-shroom says it shoots fumes that pass through screen doors, omitting AoE as secondary (28:00-29:00). 'Sophisticated caveman' voice.

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [31:00]
label: developer
claim: Crazy Dave's dialogue is broken into small chunks advanced by click. He was cut from level 1-1 and delayed five levels because introducing himself and in-character lines 'made the tutorial less direct'; early tutorials stay direct, dialogue added once players are invested (30:00-31:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [32:00]
label: developer
claim: Don't pause play for messages: dislikes OK dialogs that freeze action; prefers passively displayed text at screen bottom so play continues. Cites a side scroller with 'press Z to jump' painted on the background wall that scrolls away when no longer needed (32:00-33:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [33:00]
label: developer
claim: Adaptive tips, found by watching a friend play: he put all peashooters in the far right column and lost, so a message 'one of your peashooters has died, try planting them further to the left' shows only if a peashooter dies in the right-most columns early. Players doing it right never see it (33:00-34:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [34:00]
label: developer
claim: Let players feel smart: telling hardcore players what to do 'we don't give them the chance to feel smart' and may feel insulting, so adaptive messaging covers novices (like his mom) without that cost (34:00). Sunflower tip shown on levels 1-3 to 1-8 only if under 3 sunflowers about a minute in (35:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [35:00]
label: developer
claim: Disputes over-explaining: 'no need to explain every single concept'; most things from minute 30 on are 'better learned by experimentation instead of hand-holding' because figuring out strategies is the best part (35:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [36:00]
label: developer
claim: Escalating hints in Insaniquarium: a PopCap suggestion to hint at game start was refused as too in-your-face and robbing discovery; instead after carnivore death 1 'warning, your carnivore has died', death 2 a hint, death 3 a plain instruction. Some playtesters never figured out what to feed carnivores (35:00-37:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [37:00]
label: developer
claim: Don't create noise: avoid UI clutter, pop-ups and early achievements competing with a tutorial message; PC PvZ shipped without achievements. Irrelevant messages erode trust ('don't cry wolf') so later relevant ones get ignored (37:00-39:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [39:00]
label: developer
claim: Visuals teach: rule one, a plant or zombie should show what it does at a glance (spout, shield, spikes, three heads); rule two, at least understandable after seeing it act once (jalapeno, pole vaulter). Repeater fires volleys of two at the pea shooter's interval so double damage is visible instantly; puff-shroom has a short visible range; grave buster looks like it chews gravestones (39:00-45:00).

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [48:00]
label: developer
claim: Leverage prior knowledge: sun for plants, money for purchasing (not brains), metal beats plastic beats nothing for the first three zombies, bigger coins are worth more, descriptive names (-shroom suffix means night-only), coffee wakes mushrooms (48:00-52:00). He says many games get 'cute' with icons and add up to a confusing experience.

title: George Fan, How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012) [54:00]
label: developer
claim: Help button: it was a default placeholder, he confirmed help pages weren't required, and shipped a joke ('when the zombies show up just sit there and don't do anything you win the game'). 'We did such a good job of teaching the game already that we didn't need a Help section' (54:00). Build for ease of learning from the start, not at the last minute (53:00).

title: Frommel et al., The Effects of Context-Sensitive Tutorials in Virtual Reality Games (CHI PLAY 2017)
label: research
claim: n=39 (40 recruited, 1 excluded for discomfort; 14F/24M/1 unreported, mean age 23.56), between-subjects, random assignment, HTC Vive wave shooter MummyDefense; context-sensitive just-in-time speech bubbles vs modal 'instruction screen' parchments (advance by shooting a target) then separate practice phase; same wording; only 4 of 39 played VR regularly. Measures: SAM valence/arousal/dominance, 7-pt joy/frustration/anger/boredom, IEQ immersion, IMI interest/enjoyment, performance = levels won/tries in 5-min game, 4 subjective tutorial items. Mann-Whitney U. Context-sensitive better: valence Mdn 6.5 vs 5.0 (U=110, p=.017, r=-.38); joy 6.5 vs 5.0 (p=.002, r=-.50); frustration 2.0 vs 3.5 (p=.038, r=-.33); IMI enjoyment Mdn 6.5 vs 5.57 (p=.011, r=-.40); boredom p=.008 but Mdn 1 both and ns after removing an outlier. No difference: arousal, dominance, anger, IEQ overall (Mdn 5.69 vs 5.23, ns) and subscales, objective performance (M=.413 vs .300, ns), tutorial replays (1.35 vs 1.53), all 4 subjective performance items (p .101-.993). So better experience, no measurable better learning. Authors' limits: one simple VR game, low VR experience (novelty of speech bubbles may inflate), short lab study, performance measure 'not ideal for measuring if players learned', no mid-way design (modal screens at each new feature) tested. Authors say findings confirm Andersen et al. but 'although Andersen et al. found these effects mainly for complex games, our study showed similar effects for a rather simple game', so complexity may not be required (VR context). Skipping: 'players might rather skip tutorials they experience as low fun what could lead to players missing important information'; tutorial could not be skipped in study. They chose against modal screens in practice since 'instruction screens would actually have interrupted practice phases what can negatively affect presence and emotion'. Nothing on text reading time or auto-dismiss timers; both arms were player-paced (screen advanced by shooting a target), and the context bubbles' dismissal mechanism is not described.

title: Green, Khalifa, Barros, Togelius, Press Space To Fire: Automatic Video Game Tutorial Generation (AIIDE-17 EXAG workshop)
label: research
claim: Position paper (6 pages) proposing tutorial generation as an AI problem; no player study, no sample, no results, only a proposed GVG-AI pipeline (VGDL mechanic discovery -> mechanic graph -> grammar text). Its literature survey says tutorial effectiveness is complexity-dependent: 'the effectiveness of tutorials on gameplay depends on how complex a game is to begin with (Andersen et al. 2012), and sometimes are not useful at all. Game mechanics that are simple enough to be discovered using experimental methods may not require a tutorial to explain them' -> 'there exists mechanics that are too simple to be taught in a tutorial'. Also (via Williams 2009) active-learning tutorials may fail when 'the player never has an isolated place to practice a particularly complex skill'. Cites Andersen et al.'s 4 binary tutorial dimensions (presence, context sensitivity, freedom, availability of help), Suddaby 2012 types, Ray 2010 explorative vs modeling acquisition; its own types: instructions, examples, carefully designed experience. Cites Braid's rewind tutorial as shown 'when it is first necessary' (on first death) as an example, not evidence of effect. Says nothing on whether players read text; the only related evidence is secondhand.
